title: California SB 379: Which Cities Must Offer Instant Solar Permits
dek: SB 379 requires most California cities and larger counties to offer online, automated permits for home solar up to 38.4 kW and paired batteries.
keyPoints: Cities of 50,000+ and counties of 150,000+ had to offer automated solar permitting by September 30, 2023.
Cities between 5,000 and 50,000 people had until September 30, 2024.
Cities under 5,000 and counties under 150,000 are exempt.
Covered systems are residential solar up to 38.4 kW and storage paired with residential solar.
The CEC posts a status dashboard of about 429 non-exempt jurisdictions but does not certify compliance.

sources.title: Residential Solar Permit Program Status Dashboard
Automated Permitting for Solar Energy Systems - California Building Officials

body: Senate Bill 379 requires non-exempt California cities and counties to run an online, automated permitting platform that checks code compliance and issues permits in real time for residential solar and for energy storage paired with residential solar. If you install in California, it decides whether a standard rooftop job can be permitted in minutes or waits in a plan-review queue.

Who has to offer it. Cities with 50,000 or more residents and counties with 150,000 or more were required to have a platform by September 30, 2023. Cities with 5,000 to 50,000 residents had until September 30, 2024. Cities under 5,000 people and counties under 150,000 are exempt, so many rural county jurisdictions can still use traditional plan review. The California Energy Commission counts about 429 non-exempt jurisdictions.

What qualifies. The automated path covers residential solar systems no larger than 38.4 kilowatts, plus residential battery systems paired with solar. Larger systems, or jobs outside a platform's eligibility rules, still go through the jurisdiction's regular process.

Which platform. Jurisdictions can use SolarAPP+, which is free for jurisdictions to use, a commercial platform such as Symbium, or their own system, as long as it meets SB 379. Each jurisdiction sets up its own account, so a design that sails through in one city may hit a different checklist next door.
How to use this in your workflow:

Step 1: Check the CEC's Residential Solar Permit Program Status Dashboard for each jurisdiction you work in. It shows reporting status and which jurisdictions report having a platform. The CEC notes it does not certify whether a platform complies, so treat the dashboard as a starting point.
Step 2: Confirm directly with the building department which platform it uses and how contractors register. Ask whether a final inspection is scheduled through the same portal or separately.

Step 3: Standardize your design packages to the platform's inputs. Automated tools reject jobs for missing or inconsistent data, so equipment listings, string sizing, and battery specs should match your standard templates exactly.

Step 4: Track turnaround by jurisdiction. If a non-exempt city is still routing simple, eligible jobs to manual review, write down dates and permit numbers. Jurisdictions report data to the CEC every year through June 30, 2034, and clear records help you raise the issue with the city respectfully.
Today's next step: list the five jurisdictions where you pull the most solar permits and look each one up on the CEC dashboard.
